newsitem.title: UK: Baltic Exchange to drop its plans to restructure.
newsitem.headline: Baltic Exchange to drop its plans to restructure.

text.p: The Baltic Exchange is to drop its proposals to restructure the dry bulk shipping trading organisation after deciding it would not be able to get a required majority for its plans.

Baltic Exchange chief executive Jim Buckley told Reuters on Friday: "The directors will not put the proposals to the annual general meeting in July because it is apparent there is no consensus of opinion."

In May, Baltic Exchange chairman Eric Shawyer revealed plans to set up a new Baltic firm to continue the business. It would have been owned by a holding company which would pay into it 11.5 million stg.
Shawyer also proposed an immediate dividend, worth 5.4 million stg, to shareholders of 100 stg per share.

The moves followed the failure at last year's annual meeting to restructure the institution due to disagreements about the value of Baltic shares. That failure led to the setting up of a strategic review by management consultants Deloitte & Touche.
Deloitte recommended a dividend of about 200 to 250 stg per Baltic share in February 1997.

Buckley said the Baltic management had decided to drop its proposals after consulting members because it had become aware it would not gain the 75 percent acceptance required to change its articles of association.

He said members were split between supporters of the Baltic proposals, those backing a variant of it proposed by former chairman Peter Tudball, supporters of the Deloitte plan and those wishing to see no change at all.
The Baltic move came amid attempts by leading Exchange members to arrange talks ahead of the annual meeting to prevent a repeat of last year's failure.
Shipping broker Howe Robinson & Co Ltd had written to the 26 largest shareholders, who control nearly 50 percent of the shares, inviting them to a meeting to discuss the plans.

Howe Robinson chairman Peter Kerr-Dineen wrote in a letter seen by Reuters: "We are concerned at the damage which may result from a lack of agreement amongst the shareholders over the future direction of the Exchange."
The intent of the meeting, he wrote, was to explore ways of resolving the impasse.
Buckley welcomed the move by Kerr-Dineen and said he hoped the meeting could find a consensus among the main shareholders.
The Baltic Exchange has total assets of around 30 million stg, including liquid assets of around 18.5 million stg largely arising from the insurance settlement for the IRA bombing in April 1992.

It has 740 shareholders who hold 54,000 shares originally issued in 1900 at a value of five stg per unit and traded only among members. Their trading value had crept up to about 10 stg per share before the bombing when the Baltic's assets largely consisted of the old exchange building.

Buckley said that now that the Exchange's assets were roughly divided between the new building and the cash held as government bonds, some shareholders were trying to realise their full potential value.

The management had opposed the Deloitte plans because they would have removed the cash flow derived from the bonds and reduce the Baltic to holding just the ground floor of its present building, Buckley said.
-- Paul Berrill Reuters Shipping News + 44 171 542 4087. Fax 5017.
